hints: Look at what each reactant can do, $	ext{NH}_4^+$ can donate a proton and $	ext{CaO}$ is a basic oxide.
Check the oxidation numbers of N in $	ext{NH}_4^+$ and in $	ext{NH}_3$, they are both -3 so no electron transfer happens.
Remember the classic test for ammonium salts, warming with a base always drives off the pungent alkaline gas.
walkthrough:
**Spot the acid and the base**

Think of $	ext{NH}_4	ext{Cl}$ as the source of the acid $	ext{NH}_4^+$, and $	ext{CaO}$ as a base. In water, $	ext{CaO}$ forms $	ext{Ca(OH)}_2$, giving $	ext{OH}^-$ ions.

$$\text{CaO(s) + H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{Ca}^{2+}\text{(aq) + 2OH}^-\text{(aq)}$$

**Write the key ionic reaction**

The ammonium ion donates a proton to hydroxide to make ammonia and water. This is proton transfer, the definition of an acid-base reaction.

$$\text{NH}_4^+\text{(aq) + OH}^-\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{NH}_3\text{(g) + H}_2\text{O(l)}$$

**Rule out redox and identify gas M**

Check oxidation numbers. N is -3 in both $	ext{NH}_4^+$ and $	ext{NH}_3$, H is +1, O and Ca and Cl are unchanged. No oxidation or reduction occurs, so it cannot be redox.

Overall:
$$\text{2NH}_4\text{Cl(aq) + CaO(s)} \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2\text{(aq) + H}_2\text{O(l) + 2NH}_3\text{(g)}$$ 
So M is ammonia and the type is acid-base.

options.A: The reaction type is correct as acid-base, but M is not $	ext{N}_2$. Nitrogen stays at oxidation number -3, it is not oxidised to 0 in $	ext{N}_2$. This trap comes from confusing ammonia formation with decomposition to nitrogen.
options.B: M is correctly identified as $	ext{NH}_3$, but the type is wrong. No oxidation numbers change, so no redox occurs. Students choose this if they think any gas evolution or heating must be redox.
options.C: This is correct. Proton transfer from $	ext{NH}_4^+$ to base gives $	ext{NH}_3$ gas, so it is acid-base with M as ammonia. This is the standard laboratory preparation of ammonia from an ammonium salt.
options.D: Both parts are wrong. It is not redox because oxidation states are unchanged, and $	ext{N}_2$ is not formed here. This combines the two misconceptions about electron transfer and the product.
